NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Machine Learning for Systems (MLForSys)

MRVQ: One Resident Index for Dimension- and Rate-Elastic Vector Search

Sean Culatana Affiliation: Atlassian Affiliation: Mountain View, CA Email: sculatana@atlassian.com    Shang-En Huang Affiliation: National Taiwan University Affiliation: Taipei, Taiwan Email: sehuang@csie.ntu.edu.tw    Kang Li Affiliation: Atlassian Affiliation: Bellevue, WA Email: kli3@atlassian.com
Abstract

Dense-retrieval services must switch among embedding-prefix dimensions and index bit rates as latency, quality, and memory budgets change. Tuning a quantizer separately for each rate gives the best quality, but the retrieval tier then holds several code streams and quantizer states at once. We introduce Matryoshka Residual Vector Quantization (MRVQ), a post-hoc residual quantizer for frozen embeddings. Its maximum-rate code can be truncated two ways: dropping residual stages lowers the rate, and dropping embedding coordinates lowers the dimension. One resident artifact therefore serves every (dimension, rate) pair we evaluate. Across FiQA and NFCorpus, four embedding families, and {4,8,16}\{4,8,16\}-byte codes, MRVQ is the lowest-RAM design we evaluate. It uses 17.817.8–22.0×22.0\times less memory than three separately trained QINCo2 indices, and 1.891.89–2.02×2.02\times less than a lean shared-model steelman. The saving is not free: per-rate QINCo2 is 0.0260.026–0.1070.107 nDCG@10 better on FiQA. But MRVQ beats PQ, OPQ, and AdANNS-OPQ at matched code size. We also evaluate a low-build-cost PCA-scalar design that attains quality comparable to RaBitQ and its extension while fitting 420×420\times faster at the median. Finally, we report two negative results: QINCo2 collapses when trained at high rates, and a ranking-bound hypothesis misses its pre-specified acceptance criteria. MRVQ is therefore a low-memory operating point for elastic retrieval, not a universal quality winner.

1 Introduction

Dense retrieval is a first-class component of retrieval-augmented generation and agentic systems. For large corpora, the document embeddings and index state—rather than the query encoder—often dominate resident memory: a 768768–10241024 dimensional fp32 vector occupies 33–44 KB before indexing. That state must also support more than one operating point. Dimension elasticity uses prefixes of Matryoshka representations to trade retrieval quality for query compute and bandwidth (Kusupati et al., 2022; Rege et al., 2023); rate elasticity changes the document code size to trade quality for storage. A high-quality deployment can tune a quantizer independently for each rate, but then the retrieval tier retains several code streams and model states at once.

We ask whether a single resident document code can cover both axes. MRVQ fits a residual vector quantizer post-hoc on frozen embeddings, weighting reconstruction error across the served prefix dimensions. Residual stages provide nested rates, and coordinate prefixes provide nested dimensions, so the same stored code supports every (m,b)∈ℳ×ℬ(m,b)\in\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{B} (Figure 1). This differs from AdANNS, which targets dimension-adaptive search, and from MatQuant, which nests model-weight precision rather than document-index codes (Nair et al., 2025); Appendix E places MRVQ among quantizers for approximate search.

Our contribution is a systems trade-off, not a claim of universal quality dominance. First, we formalize resident-memory accounting for a full rate menu and show that one MRVQ artifact is the lowest-RAM configuration evaluated. Second, we measure the corresponding quality cost against QINCo2 and the gains over standard ANN quantizers. Third, we evaluate a separate, inexpensive PCA-scalar design for hosts on which iterative quantizer training is undesirable. Finally, we report two negative results—high-rate QINCo2 training failures and a ranking-preservation predictor that does not meet our pre-specified bar.

2 MRVQ and Resident-Memory Model

Let {xi}i=1n⊂ℝD\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{D} be frozen document embeddings. An LL-stage residual vector quantizer with K=256K=256 codewords per stage produces indices zi(1:L)z_{i}^{(1:L)} and reconstructions x^i(ℓ)=∑j=1ℓCzi(j)(j)\hat{x}_{i}^{(\ell)}=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}C^{(j)}_{z_{i}^{(j)}}. Because each stage index occupies one byte, decoding the first bb stages gives a bb-byte code. MRVQ makes the same code dimension-elastic by fitting the codebooks under

ℒprefix=∑i=1n∑m∈ℳwm‖xi[:m]−x^i(L)[:m]‖22,wm≥0,∑mwm=1.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prefix}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}w_{m}\left\|x_{i}^{[:m]}-\hat{x}_{i}^{(L)[:m]}\right\|_{2}^{2},\qquad w_{m}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{m}w_{m}=1. (1)

At serving time, (m,b)(m,b) selects x^i(b)[:m]\hat{x}_{i}^{(b)[:m]}; no re-encoding and no additional document code is required. Queries remain in floating point and are scored asymmetrically, as in PQ/OPQ and RaBitQ.

For the evaluated L=16L=16, MRVQ’s resident state is RMRVQ=4​L​K​D+16​nR_{\mathrm{MRVQ}}=4LKD+16n bytes: fp32 codebooks plus one 1616-byte code per vector. A deployment with a separate QINCo2 artifact for each b∈ℬ={4,8,16}b\in\mathcal{B}=\{4,8,16\} costs Rsep=∑b∈ℬ(Pb+n​b)R_{\mathrm{sep}}=\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}(P_{b}+nb), where PbP_{b} is the corresponding model state; a shared-model steelman costs Rshared=P16+16​nR_{\mathrm{shared}}=P_{16}+16n. The document-code term alone therefore changes from 28​n28n to 16​n16n bytes (1.75×1.75\times asymptotically), and at the corpus sizes we evaluate, sharing the fixed quantizer state produces a much larger ratio. Appendix A reports the fixed and per-vector terms separately so the accounting can be checked at any nn.

We also study a separate PCA-scalar operating point: rotate by PCA, allocate scalar bits by coordinate variance, and quantize each coordinate independently. It requires an eigendecomposition but no iterative learned-codebook training; it is not included in the MRVQ memory accounting.

3 Evaluation

We use FiQA (57,63857{,}638 documents, 648648 queries) and NFCorpus (3,6333{,}633 documents, 323323 queries) from BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021). The four embedding families are MPNet (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) (D=768D=768), Mxbai (Lee et al., 2024) (D=1024D=1024), Nomic (Nussbaum et al., 2024) (D=768D=768), and BGE (Xiao et al., 2023) (D=768D=768). Within each family, every method uses the same fixed, model-specific prefix menu ℳ⊆{128,256,384,512,768,1024}\mathcal{M}\subseteq\{128,256,384,512,768,1024\}, and a “menu mean” is the unweighted mean over that family’s evaluated prefix-rate cells. The prefix weights wmw_{m} in Eq. (1) are uniform over ℳ\mathcal{M} and all 1616 residual stages are weighted equally; Appendix F lists the exact checkpoints, menus, and fitting budget. Rates are ℬ={4,8,16}\mathcal{B}=\{4,8,16\} B/vector, or 192192–1024×1024\times smaller than the corresponding fp32 vector before fixed quantizer overhead.

The metric is nDCG@10. Learned baselines use matched fitting budgets, and their aggregated per-rate results reproduce the stored runs to floating-point tolerance (maximum absolute deviation 00 for MRVQ, 5×10−175\times 10^{-17} for QINCo2). We use paired per-query bootstrap confidence intervals (50005000 resamples; 10,00010{,}000 for the RaBitQ study). Decision thresholds for the negative-result tests were fixed before the final aggregate analyses. Reported RAM is analytical accounting from the byte formulas above—parameter and code bytes only, with no optimizer or runtime buffers—rather than measured process RSS.

4 Results

One artifact is the low-RAM corner.

Table 1 prices the complete {4,8,16}\{4,8,16\} B/vector menu. MRVQ uses 12.0612.06–16.8816.88 MiB and is the lowest-RAM configuration for all four families on both datasets. Relative to three separate QINCo2 models, the saving is 17.817.8–22.0×22.0\times; relative to the leanest shared-model configuration (including reduced embedding width and fp16 variants), it is 1.891.89–2.02×2.02\times. The first ratio is largest at these on-device and per-tenant corpus scales because neural parameter state dominates the resident footprint (Appendix A). As nn grows, the separate-model ratio approaches the 28/16=1.75×28/16=1.75\times code-stream ratio, while the shared-model gap becomes a fixed overhead and therefore less important; Figure 2(b) makes both limits explicit.

Quality forms a two-corner Pareto.

At matched code size, separately trained QINCo2 (Huijben et al., 2024; Vallaeys et al., 2025) beats MRVQ in every FiQA family-rate cell by 0.0260.026–0.1070.107 nDCG@10 (Appendix B). Conversely, even the shared-model QINCo2 steelman uses roughly 1.9×1.9\times MRVQ’s RAM at the evaluated corpus sizes. Figure 2(a) therefore shows two useful operating points rather than a single winner. The low-memory result repeats on NFCorpus for all four families.

Against standard fixed-code ANN baselines, MRVQ is stronger at matched bytes. Across the aggressive 44–1616 B/vector regime, paired-bootstrap intervals favor MRVQ over per-prefix OPQ by about 0.060.06–0.070.07 nDCG@10, over PQ by 0.100.10–0.120.12, and over AdANNS-OPQ (Rege et al., 2023) in every evaluated cell. The practical rule is therefore constraint-dependent: choose QINCo2 when quality dominates, and MRVQ when resident memory prevents keeping several specialized artifacts.

A low-build-cost scalar alternative.

We compare PCA-scalar with RaBitQ and Extended-RaBitQ (Gao and Long, 2024; Gao et al., 2024) using native Faiss 1.13.2 asymmetric cosine search on ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized vectors. At nominal b∈{1,2,4}b\in\{1,2,4\} bits/dimension, the RaBitQ representation receives an additional 8/20/208/20/20 B/vector, so the byte accounting is conservative for PCA-scalar. Across the two aggregate query grids, pooled PCA-scalar −- RaBitQ deltas are +0.0076/+0.0029/+0.0010+0.0076/+0.0029/+0.0010 and −0.0009/+0.0012/+0.0006-0.0009/+0.0012/+0.0006 nDCG@10 at b=1/2/4b=1/2/4. All absolute effects are below 0.0080.008, and one Mxbai 11-bit cell favors RaBitQ by 0.00390.0039; we therefore describe quality as comparable, not superior. Timed separately on three held-out BEIR corpora (1818 cells, fixed 88-thread CPU), PCA training is 420×420\times faster than matched OPQ fitting at the median and 686×686\times at the mean, with a 4747–1967×1967\times spread: 0.170.17–6.956.95 s against 7272–416416 s. That makes it attractive for in-place rebuilds (Appendix C).

5 Limitations and Conclusion

Training reliability.

On NFCorpus at 1616 stages, per-rate QINCo2 suffers retrieval collapse—nDCG@10 below half the MRVQ value despite converged validation MSE—in 3/33/3 BGE seeds (best 0.0350.035) and 1/31/3 Nomic seeds. The best surviving Nomic seed is also non-monotone in rate: 0.2940.294 at 1616 stages against 0.3200.320 at 88. We retain these failures rather than silently dropping them.

No ranking certificate.

A parameter-free predictor based on residual energy is directionally useful but misses our pre-specified acceptance bar: pooled rank correlation is 0.8250.825 against a required 0.850.85, and only 72%72\% of cells yield a non-vacuous bound against a required 90%90\% (Appendix D).

Scope.

The quality study covers two modest BEIR corpora and four embedding families. We measure resident memory and ranking quality, not end-to-end ANN latency, build energy, or recall–throughput curves; the RAM gains should not be read as speedups. At very large nn the advantage over a shared-model baseline narrows as the accounting predicts.

Within that scope, MRVQ converts a dimension-and-rate menu from several rate-specialized resident artifacts into one post-hoc code. It pays a measurable quality cost to QINCo2, but beats standard ANN quantizers at matched bytes and occupies a distinct low-memory Pareto point. That is the intended systems contribution: a simple deployment option for elastic retrieval when resident memory, rather than peak quality, is the binding resource.

Appendix A Resident-memory accounting and scaling

Table 2 separates each configuration’s resident state into a fixed term and a per-vector term, so Table 1 can be reconstructed at any corpus size. The MRVQ fixed term is 4​L​K​D4LKD bytes exactly. The separate-rate QINCo2 term counts three rate-specific models (de=Dd_{e}\!=\!D, dh=256d_{h}\!=\!256, K=256K\!=\!256, A=16A\!=\!16, B=32B\!=\!32, two sub-layers, fp32); at D=768D\!=\!768 these hold 7.287.28M, 16.7216.72M, and 35.6035.60M parameters, so 4​∑bPb=227.34\sum_{b}P_{b}=227.3 MiB. The shared-model steelman is a single maximum-rate QINCo2 with de=128d_{e}\!=\!128 in fp16, prefix-truncated to serve 4/8/164/8/16 B/vector. All terms count parameter bytes only. Figure 3 shows the resulting split at FiQA scale, where the fixed state accounts for over 93%93\% of resident bytes in every configuration.

Because MRVQ and the shared-model steelman carry the same 16​n16n slope, their difference is a constant 12.2912.29 MiB at D=768D=768: MRVQ stays more than 1.1×1.1\times smaller through n≈7.3n\approx 7.3M vectors, and the gap is under 8%8\% beyond about 1010M vectors. The separate-rate menu instead carries a 28​n28n slope, so its ratio to MRVQ decays toward 28/16=1.75×28/16=1.75\times rather than to parity.

Appendix B Full matched-byte quality grid

Table 3 reports FiQA MRVQ −- QINCo2 nDCG@10 at matched code size. All paired-bootstrap intervals favor QINCo2; the values quantify the quality cost of sharing one code across the whole menu.

Appendix C PCA-scalar versus RaBitQ

Figure 4 plots the matched-nominal-bit deltas summarized in Section 4. The pre-specified practical-equivalence band was ±0.005\pm 0.005 nDCG@10. The pooled results are small, but the 11-bit small-grid mean and its whole confidence interval lie above that band, which is why the main text says “comparable” rather than claiming formal equivalence. Note also that the two grids disagree in sign at 11 bit.

The fitting-speed comparison is timed on ArguAna, Quora, and SciDocs rather than on FiQA and NFCorpus, so it characterizes the two fitting procedures rather than the specific indices evaluated above. Across those 1818 cells, PCA training takes 0.170.17–6.956.95 s against 7272–416416 s for matched OPQ fitting; the ratio has median 420×420\times and mean 686×686\times, ranging from 47×47\times to 1967×1967\times. We quote the median in the main text because the mean is inflated by the largest corpus-model pairs.

Appendix D Ranking-preservation predictor

The tested predictor is ϵ⁡(r)=D⁡(r)\epsilon(r)=\sqrt{D(r)}, where D⁡(r)=𝔼i​‖xi−xi(r)‖22D(r)=\mathbb{E}_{i}\|x_{i}-x_{i}^{(r)}\|_{2}^{2} and ‖q‖2=1\|q\|_{2}=1; Cauchy–Schwarz then bounds RMS score perturbation by ϵ⁡(r)\epsilon(r). The sweep covers 4040 cells: two datasets, four families, and five rates {1,2,4,8,16}\{1,2,4,8,16\} B/vector. This rate set deliberately extends below the ℬ={4,8,16}\mathcal{B}=\{4,8,16\} serving menu of the main text, because a bound that is only meaningful at generous rates would be of little use. Fixed-rate cross-geometry Spearman correlation is 0.660.66, pooled predictor–gap Spearman correlation is 0.8250.825, and only 72%72\% of cells have a non-vacuous bound. Both aggregate statistics miss the pre-specified acceptance thresholds. Normalizing by 𝔼​‖x‖22\mathbb{E}\|x\|_{2}^{2} removes a scale confound from unnormalized Mxbai embeddings but does not change the verdict.

Appendix E Related work

PQ, OPQ, and additive quantization are standard fixed-rate compressors [Jégou et al., 2011, Ge et al., 2013, Babenko and Lempitsky, 2014]. QINCo/QINCo2 use implicit neural codebooks to improve rate–distortion performance [Huijben et al., 2024, Vallaeys et al., 2025]. RaBitQ and its extension provide scalar-quantization methods with error guarantees [Gao and Long, 2024, Gao et al., 2024]. Matryoshka representation learning and AdANNS expose dimension elasticity [Kusupati et al., 2022, Rege et al., 2023], while MatQuant nests model-weight bit widths [Nair et al., 2025]. MRVQ instead targets the resident document index: one post-hoc code is truncated along both the residual-stage and the embedding-coordinate axis.
